(out/'manuscript.txt').write_text('\\n\\n'.join(f'=== PAGE {i+1} ===\\n'+p.read_text() for i,p in enumerate(sorted(out.glob('page-*.txt')))))

strengths: LPAM addresses a practical stitching problem: seam selection cannot repair substantial local misalignment. Restricting additional alignment to problematic seam regions offers a useful, training-free extension to existing pipelines.

The experiments cover 79 image pairs across three datasets, four seam-cutting methods, and five alignment methods, including UDIS++. Tables 1–2 show consistent improvements; for example, baseline SSIM on SEAGULL increases from 0.638 to 0.697.

Figures 1, 5, and 7 demonstrate visible repairs to structural discontinuities. The sigmoid ablation and the candid small-patch failure discussion help explain the alignment-versus-boundary-consistency tradeoff.
The overview and pseudocode make the core workflow understandable. Established components and public datasets are cited, and a code repository is provided.
weaknesses: The quantitative evidence does not adequately establish improved overall mosaic quality. Equations (6)–(9) measure agreement between source patches along the resulting seam, leaving distortion and artifacts elsewhere unmeasured. Table 3 exposes this mismatch: removing the sigmoid improves RMSE, SSIM, and ZNCC on all three datasets, although Figure 3 shows undesirable boundary artifacts. The authors recognize this issue, but systematic perceptual or boundary-quality evaluation and per-image failure statistics are needed to substantiate the broader quality and robustness claims.

The contribution beyond existing seam-guided alignment is insufficiently established. The manuscript itself describes adaptive alignment in SEAGULL [22] and dense-flow-based seam estimation in [35], making its blanket characterization of prior approaches as operating on settled pre-aligned images too strong. Figure 7 provides a selected visual comparison with full stitching pipelines, but there is no quantitative comparison with these closely related approaches or controlled comparison against dense refinement over the entire seam. Such evidence would clarify the value of selective local compensation.

The seam acceptance rule in Section 3.2 can skip uniformly poor seams. For example, if every pixel has Q = 0.8, max(Q) ≤ 1.5 mean(Q) holds and no repair occurs despite uniformly low SSIM. This is a concrete limitation relevant to poor initial alignment, and neither sensitivity to k nor performance under widespread misalignment is evaluated. The claim that LPAM dissociates seam quality from initial alignment accuracy therefore exceeds the demonstrated scope.

The boundary-consistency claim is stronger than the formulation supports. At the default beta = 8, Equation (5) gives approximately 0.018 and 0.982 at the two endpoints, and the horizontal ramp does not enforce continuity around every boundary of a rectangular patch. Preserving boundary source labels also does not guarantee matching pixel values after warping. Figure 6 usefully acknowledges failures, but explicit boundary handling or broader validation is needed to support seamless integration across arbitrary seam geometries.

Reproducibility and efficiency reporting remain incomplete. Alignment-patch padding, overlapping-patch handling, SIFT-flow settings, and input resolutions are insufficiently specified. Table 4 reports seam-cutting and LPAM times separately, so its '+LPAM' entries should not be read as total pipeline times; for example, the SEAGULL baseline would increase from 4.11 to approximately 11.45 seconds. Clear total timings and comparisons with alternative refinement strategies would better support the lightweight-efficiency claim.
